new_statements.quote: In het lonkundó valt het intensiteitsaccent gewoonlijk op de eerste klankgreep van den stam. [...] i-ˈlombɛ, huis; bo-ˈkulaka, rijk man; á-ˈsanga, hij zegt; baô-ˈtúngama, zij zijn gevangen. Soms, doch zelden, op de laatste; bv. bokɛˈlé, ei; lokoˈlé, trommel. Eénklankgrepige stammen hebben het krachtaccent op het prefix, tenzij er een suffix op volgt; bv. ˈbo-nto, mensch; ˈá-yá, hij komt; maar: á-ˈyá-kí, hij kwam. Afleidingen vertoonen meerdere uitzonderingen op deze regels; dikwijls is de voorlaatste klankgreep van het achtervoegsel beklemtoond [...] het intensiteitsaccent gaat niet noodzakelijkerwijze met een hoogeren muzikalen toon gepaard
new_statements.translation: In Lonkundo the intensity accent usually falls on the first syllable of the stem. [...] i-'lombe house; bo-'kulaka rich man; a-'sanga he says; bao-'tungama they are caught. Sometimes, but rarely, on the last; e.g. boke'le egg; loko'le drum. Monosyllabic stems have the stress accent on the prefix, unless a suffix follows; e.g. 'bo-nto person; 'a-ya he comes; but a-'ya-ki he came. Derivations show several exceptions to these rules; often the penultimate syllable of the suffix is stressed [...] the intensity accent does not necessarily go together with a higher musical tone

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mongo (Lonkundo) has a tone system plus a weaker dynamic stress that falls, as a rule, on the first syllable of the stem (root), independent of tone; rarely word-final; monosyllabic stems throw it onto the prefix unless a suffix follows; derived stems often stress the penult of the suffix; each element of a compound keeps its own stress. Nothing is published about the Yamongeri variety in particular.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; Hulstaert says a word has one stressed syllable 'soms twee' (sometimes two), and compounds/onomatopoeia keep one stress per member (ˈbón-ˈlólu 'youth', eˈkamb-aˈkula 'arrow-dodger').
new_statements.exceptions: Rare stem-final stress (bokɛlé 'egg', lokolé 'drum'); monosyllabic stems (stress on prefix, shifting to the stem when a suffix is added: ˈá-yá vs á-ˈyá-kí); derivations often stress the penult of the suffix (elaˈngélá, átosaˈngélé).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (stem/prefix/suffix), citation forms in a pedagogical grammar of Lonkundo/Lomongo; stress is described as less prominent than tone and not tied to high tone. Applies to Mongo generally; the source never mentions the Yamongeri.
new_statements.identity_note: yamo1246 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping entry (ISO ymg still Active). Glottolog: the group is located south of the Congo river in Equateur (Hackett & van Bulck 1956: 72) and 'speaks a variety of Mongo [lol]' (Hulstaert 1999) = mong1338. But Maho 2009 NUGL puts 'C36H Yamongeri' in the Losengo cluster, Ethnologue 16 classifies it Bangi-Ntomba and says 'related to Budza [bja]', Ethnologue 22 says Bangi-Ntomba (C.36). No source names the Yamongeri in any linguistic description held by the project (Hulstaert 1999 dialectology, Motingea 1990, Motingea 1995 all silent). The quoted statement is for Mongo/Lonkundo (mong1338), already in the catalog under that code; it applies to the Yamongeri only on Glottolog's say-so.

sources.note: Mongo (Lonkundo), not Yamongeri: intensity accent usually on the first syllable of the stem; rarely on the last (bokelé, lokolé); monosyllabic stems stress the prefix unless a suffix follows; derivations often stress the penult of the suffix; each member of a compound keeps its own accent; accent is independent of tone. Already the catalog quote for mong1338.

sources.citation: De Rop, A. 1958. Grammaire du Lomongo: phonologie et morphologie. Léopoldville: Université Lovanium. Chap. IV 'L'accent d'intensité', pp. 10-11.
sources.note: Mongo, not Yamongeri: 'En général l'accent d'intensité porte sur la première syllabe du radical' (p. 10), rarely on the last syllable of the radical; monosyllabic radicals stress the prefix; derivation often shifts stress to the penult; compounds keep each member's accent (p. 11). Same rule as Hulstaert 1938, cited there.
